title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing -- July 27, 2026
headline: All twenty scores confirmed tonight; a private prison operator's apparent gain was a stored math error.
summary: Twenty governments, cities, and companies were reviewed overnight, the fourth and final night of a four-night catch-up review. All twenty scores held within the benchmark's five-point confirmation range, and no bands changed. The one score that looked different, GEO Group at plus 5.3 points, turned out to be a stored math error, not better conduct. The private prison operator's own numbers add up to 12.5, not its published 6.6, so the gap was flagged for correction, not reported as improvement. For a fourth night running, an old news event was nearly scored as if it happened this month. Each time, a second check caught the wrong date before it reached a published score. India's government met all three protester demands after a violent police crackdown, but the movement stayed below the threshold for a formal score change. Eight of tonight's twenty reviews turned on one question: whose conduct was this, really? Floods, a lender's decision, and another city's protest were all set aside as not the scored entity's own doing. None of the eight change proposals already waiting in the queue from earlier this week were touched tonight.

pipeline.queueHandling: All twenty assessments confirmed within the five-point range and zero change proposals were generated. GEO Group's apparent plus 5.3 movement was traced to a stored composite error and referred for index maintenance rather than reported as a score change. All eight proposals already in the queue from the prior three nights remain pending and untouched: Baxter International at 60.9, Guinea-Bissau at 20.3, Becton Dickinson at 54.1, Ecuador at 35.9, Microsoft AI at 81.4, Tunis at 34.4, Uganda at 20.3, and Kathmandu at 18.8.

topSignals.title: GEO Group's Score Looked 5.3 Points Better Tonight. It Was a Stored Math Error, Not Improved Conduct.
topSignals.whyItMatters: A number moving up does not always mean an institution got better. GEO Group's own eight published dimension scores add up to 12.5 out of 100, not its published 6.6, so the benchmark treated the gap as a data error, not a finding of progress.
topSignals.description: GEO Group's published score is 6.6 out of 100. Tonight's review found 11.9, a movement of plus 5.3, which numerically crosses the benchmark's threshold for a formal score-change proposal. No proposal was filed, because the movement is not real. GEO Group's own eight published dimension scores are all 1.5 out of 5, and the benchmark's standard formula turns that set of numbers into a composite of 12.5, not 6.6. An independent automated check of the published index confirms the same 5.9-point gap. Tonight's assessed figure of 11.9 is close to the mathematically correct value of GEO Group's own stored numbers, not evidence that the company treats detained people any better than before. The company's weakest areas, on a five-point scale, remain Awareness, Empathy, Equity, Accountability, and Integrity, all near the bottom at 1.4. A Cal/OSHA workplace-safety settlement over conditions at a California detention facility, which a news article had suggested was recent, was in fact signed in May and reported before this review's window opened, so it was set aside as background rather than scored as new conduct. The only in-window event found was Citizens Bank ending its lending relationship with GEO Group and CoreCivic on business grounds, which is the bank's decision, not GEO Group's conduct. The 5.9-point gap between GEO Group's published score and its own numbers has been sent to the benchmark's maintenance team for correction.

evidence.claim: Citizens Bank ended its lending relationships with GEO Group and CoreCivic on July 17, 2026, citing changed commercial circumstances rather than political pressure, since the federal government has been buying detention facilities directly.

GEO Group's eight published dimension scores are all 1.5 out of 5, which the benchmark's standard formula converts to a composite of 12.5 out of 100, not the company's published 6.6 -- a five-point-nine gap confirmed by an independent automated check of the index.

topSignals.title: Every Score Held Tonight, and the Discipline That Kept It That Way Is the Story
topSignals.whyItMatters: Delhi's police crackdown was serious enough that a large score drop would have been easy to justify. Instead, the review was anchored to the last assessment so the number reflects new evidence, not a different reviewer's judgment call.
topSignals.description: Twenty entities were reviewed tonight and all twenty confirmed within the benchmark's five-point range, with zero score changes and zero band changes. Delhi is the clearest example of why that happened by design, not by accident. Human Rights Watch found that on July 20, 2026, security forces used tear gas and batons against a peaceful march on Parliament and shut down mobile internet across central Delhi, verified through nine witness interviews and ten videos. A hunger-striking activist was forcibly hospitalized on July 18. Reviewed from scratch, that evidence could plausibly support a score roughly six and a half points lower than published. Instead, the review was anchored to Delhi's own assessment from one week earlier and moved only the parts of the score with direct new evidence behind them, producing a smaller, four-point-seven-point drop. The gap between those two numbers is not new conduct: it is the normal variation between two reviewers looking at the same city, and the benchmark's rule is to use the anchored, more conservative number rather than let re-measurement alone move a score.

evidence.claim: On July 20, 2026, Delhi security forces used tear gas and batons against a peaceful student march on Parliament and shut down mobile internet in central Delhi; Human Rights Watch verified the events through nine witness interviews and ten videos.
Authorities suspended metro services and mobile internet and installed barricades to prevent marchers from reaching Parliament.

topSignals.title: For a Fourth Night Running, the Benchmark Caught Its Own Scanner Citing Old News as Current
topSignals.whyItMatters: A federal finding from June was almost scored as July conduct, for the fourth night in a row. The scanner cannot always tell an old event from a new one just by looking at a web address, so a second read keeps catching it first.
topSignals.description: Four items were corrected or dropped tonight on date-verification grounds, extending a pattern now seen on four consecutive nights (five items July 24, two items July 25, six items July 26, four items July 27). UnitedHealth Group: a federal finding that UnitedHealthcare denied 71 percent of long-term acute-care hospital admission requests was published by the HHS Office of Inspector General on June 8, 2026, not in July as an article had implied; the true in-window event is a mid-July Senate records demand, which is what was actually scored. GEO Group: a Cal/OSHA workplace-safety settlement reported on July 7 was actually signed in May 2026, both before the review window opened; dropped as background. Atlanta: a widely reported one-billion-dollar detention-warehouse plan abandonment turned out to be a June 2026 event in Social Circle, Georgia, a separate town of about 5,000 people, not the City of Atlanta; dropped on both date and location grounds. Afghanistan: reported figures of roughly 80 injured and more than 100 missing from flash floods could not be tied to any dated statement and were not scored; the United Nations' verified count of 26 killed and nine injured was used instead. None of the four reached a published score.

evidence.claim: The finding that UnitedHealthcare denied 71 percent of long-term acute-care hospital admission requests was published by the HHS Office of Inspector General on June 8, 2026, not in July; the in-window event actually scored is a mid-July Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations records demand.

A roughly one-billion-dollar detention-warehouse expansion abandonment reported this cycle actually concerns Social Circle, Georgia, a separate municipality of about 5,000 people, and the plan was ended in June 2026, not July.

topSignals.title: Eight Findings Tonight Turned on Whose Conduct It Actually Was
topSignals.whyItMatters: Floods, a bank's lending decision, and marches in cities hundreds of miles from a police crackdown were all real events tonight. None of them moved a score, because the benchmark scores an entity for its own conduct, not for harm that happened nearby or was caused by someone else.
topSignals.description: The benchmark's attribution rule was applied to eight entities tonight. Afghanistan: flash floods are a natural hazard, not government conduct, so only detection, warning, response and repair capacity were scored, with the response led by UN agencies and NGOs rather than the state. Sudan: donor countries cutting aid funding is donor conduct, not Sudan's; Sudan's score continues to reflect its own famine-related governance. Mumbai and Kolkata: the documented excessive force against protesters happened in Delhi, roughly 1,400 kilometers away, carried out by Delhi Police; both cities only hosted peaceful solidarity demonstrations, with no evidence of force by their own police. Lahore: a nationwide monsoon death toll of 109 since late June, concentrated hundreds of kilometers away in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, was not attributed to Lahore; only the city's own drainage failures were scored. Guatemala City: the judicial persecution of a journalist and the exile of dozens of judges and prosecutors is conduct by Guatemala's national Public Ministry and courts, not the municipal government. Detroit and Atlanta: federal immigration-enforcement conduct, including a paused-then-reversed vehicle-pursuit policy and a vigil outside a federal ICE office, is not city conduct in either case. GEO Group: a bank's decision to stop lending to a company is the bank's conduct, not the company's.

evidence.claim: Solidarity demonstrations tied to the national exam-leak protest movement spread to Mumbai and Kolkata alongside Bengaluru, Patna and Ahmedabad, with no documented use of force by either city's own police.

topSignals.title: India Met All Three Protester Demands This Week, But Its Score Barely Moved
topSignals.whyItMatters: A government resigning a minister and accepting every protester demand is a real concession. Because the entity's score is currently being pulled down by the police violence that provoked those protests, the improvement stayed too small to trigger a formal score change.
topSignals.description: India's education minister resigned on July 25, 2026, and the government accepted all three demands raised by protesting students: the resignation itself, compensation for the families of students who died by suicide after exam retakes, and no punitive action against protesters. Tonight's review found this is real, verified, in-window government conduct, not evidence dredged up to justify a pre-decided score. It moved India's composite up by 1.3 points, from 15.6 to 16.9. That is below the benchmark's five-point line for a formal score-change proposal, and India's overall record this cycle was dominated by the crackdown that produced the protests in the first place: tear gas and batons used against a peaceful march, an internet shutdown, and the forced hospitalization of a hunger-striking activist. Because the entity surfaced in this review on that negative evidence, the smaller positive movement was recorded and confirmed rather than proposed as an upgrade.

evidence.claim: India's education minister resigned on July 25, 2026, and the government accepted all three demands raised by the protest movement: the resignation, compensation for affected families, and no punitive action against protesters.

methodologyNotes.name: A Fourth Consecutive Night of Catching the Benchmark's Own Scanner Citing Old News as Current
methodologyNotes.description: For a fourth night running, the benchmark's nightly news scan cited an event that had already happened as if it were new: a federal finding about UnitedHealth Group from June, a settlement signed in May, and an unrelated municipality's story were all nearly scored as this month's conduct. This class of error is now a recurring pattern across four straight nights. The current check cannot always tell an old event from a new one just by looking at a web address; it works by verifying the true publish date of each individual source before anything is scored. A second read caught all four instances tonight before they reached a published score, which is what the check is designed to do.

methodologyNotes.name: A Number Moving Up Doesn't Always Mean an Institution Improved
methodologyNotes.description: GEO Group's score looked 5.3 points better tonight, which would normally be enough to trigger a formal review of whether to raise its published score. It was not, because the underlying numbers do not support it: the company's own eight published scores add up to 12.5 out of 100 using the benchmark's standard formula, not its published 6.6. The gap is an arithmetic error in how the score was stored, not evidence that the company treats the people in its custody any better. The benchmark declined to report an improvement that was really a data error, and sent the gap to be corrected instead.

methodologyNotes.name: Reviewing a City Again Starts From Its Last Score, Not From Zero
methodologyNotes.description: When an entity that was assessed recently comes up for review again, the benchmark starts from that recent score and moves it only where there is direct new evidence, rather than re-deriving every part of the score from scratch. Delhi is the example tonight: a from-scratch re-derivation of the same evidence could plausibly have produced a larger score drop than the smaller, anchored one that was actually used. The difference between the two is normal variation between reviewers, not new conduct, and the benchmark's rule is to use the more conservative, anchored figure.

methodologyNotes.name: Conduct Is Scored, Not Proximity to Harm
methodologyNotes.description: The benchmark scores what a government, city or company does, not what happens near it or because of someone else's decision. Tonight this rule applied to eight entities: Afghanistan (floods), Sudan (donor funding cuts), Mumbai and Kolkata (protests policed in another city), Lahore (a nationwide toll concentrated elsewhere), Guatemala City (national judicial conduct), Detroit and Atlanta (federal enforcement policy), and GEO Group (a lender's decision) were all held to their own documented conduct rather than events that happened to, near, or because of them.
